questions.title: Which nucleus lies in the floor of the fourth ventricle and is vulnerable to a fourth-ventricle tumour?
questions.question: A tumour expanding within the fourth ventricle classically affects which cranial nerve nucleus first, because of its location in the ventricular floor?

explanations.A: Correct. The abducens nucleus lies in the caudal pons, directly beneath the facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle. This superficial position makes it especially vulnerable to compression by an expanding fourth-ventricle mass, producing an ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy, sometimes with associated facial weakness from the adjacent facial nerve genu.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The oculomotor nucleus lies in the midbrain tegmentum, at the level of the superior colliculus, well away from the fourth ventricle floor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The trochlear nucleus lies in the midbrain, at the inferior collicular level, not in the fourth ventricle floor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The hypoglossal nucleus does lie near the floor of the fourth ventricle but more caudally, in the medulla; the classically taught landmark directly beneath the facial colliculus is the abducens nucleus.

questions.learning_objective: State that the abducens nucleus sits in the floor of the fourth ventricle and is therefore vulnerable to fourth-ventricle tumours.

questions.title: Which cortical area is classically described as formulating thoughts prior to their conversion into speech?
questions.question: Which cortical language area is classically described as the site where thoughts are formulated, before being relayed to Broca's area for conversion into speech?

explanations.A: Correct. Wernicke's area, in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, is classically described as the general interpretative (gnostic) area where language content is analysed for meaning and coherent thoughts are formulated, before being relayed via the arcuate fasciculus to Broca's area for conversion into articulate speech. A lesion here produces fluent but meaningless (receptive) aphasia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Broca's area converts already-formulated thoughts into the motor programme for speech articulation; it does not itself formulate the thought content.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The angular gyrus is a parietal association area involved in reading and cross-modal language association, not primary thought formulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The primary motor cortex executes the motor commands for speech muscles; it plays no role in formulating linguistic thought content.

questions.learning_objective: State that Wernicke's area is responsible for formulating thoughts prior to their conversion into speech by Broca's area.

questions.title: Which drug is used to abort an acute panic attack?
questions.question: A patient presents with an acute panic attack. Which drug is used to rapidly abort the episode?

explanations.A: Correct. Alprazolam, a short-acting, high-potency benzodiazepine, rapidly potentiates GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibition and has a fast enough onset to abort an acute panic attack, unlike the delayed-onset agents used for chronic panic-disorder prophylaxis. This rapid onset is the key advantage over slower-acting agents in this acute setting.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sertraline (an SSRI) is used for long-term panic disorder prophylaxis but has a delayed onset of action (weeks), making it unsuitable for aborting an acute attack.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Propranolol can blunt the somatic (autonomic) symptoms of anxiety but is not the rapid-onset agent of choice for terminating an acute panic attack.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buspirone is a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic with a slow onset of action over one to two weeks, unsuitable for acute panic attacks.

questions.learning_objective: Identify alprazolam as the benzodiazepine used to abort an acute panic attack.

questions.title: The great cerebral vein of Galen is formed by the union of which two veins?
questions.question: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum by the union of which pair of veins?

options.B: The two basal veins of Rosenthal

explanations.A: Correct. The great cerebral vein of Galen is formed beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum by the union of the two internal cerebral veins, which drain the deep structures of the cerebral hemispheres; it also receives the paired basal veins of Rosenthal before joining the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus. This deep venous confluence is clinically important because thrombosis here has serious consequences distinct from superficial cortical vein pathology.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The basal veins of Rosenthal drain into the great cerebral vein as tributaries; they are not the pair of veins whose union directly forms it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior cerebral veins are superficial cortical veins that drain into the superior sagittal sinus, unrelated to the deep venous system forming the vein of Galen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no paired "inferior cerebral vein" that forms the great cerebral vein; deep cerebral venous drainage is via the internal cerebral veins.

questions.title: Which white-matter tract completes the Papez circuit by connecting the cingulate gyrus back to the hippocampal formation?
questions.question: Which white-matter bundle, running within the cingulate gyrus, closes the Papez circuit by carrying fibres back down toward the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampal formation?

explanations.A: Correct. The cingulum is a white-matter bundle running within the cingulate gyrus that projects fibres from the cingulate cortex back down to the parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampal formation, anatomically closing the Papez circuit loop and allowing it to recirculate and sustain emotional tone. This closure is what allows the circuit to recirculate and sustain emotional tone over time.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fornix carries fibres from the hippocampus forward to the mammillary bodies, an earlier segment of the circuit, not the return connection from the cingulate gyrus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The mammillothalamic tract carries fibres from the mammillary bodies to the anterior thalamic nucleus, a different segment of the circuit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The stria terminalis connects the amygdala to the hypothalamus and septal area; it is not part of the Papez circuit's cingulate-to-hippocampus return pathway.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cingulum as the white-matter tract that completes the Papez circuit by connecting the cingulate gyrus back toward the hippocampal formation.

questions.title: Which vascular lesion, caused by chronic hypertension, classically ruptures to cause deep hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage?
questions.question: Chronic, poorly controlled hypertension classically produces which microscopic vascular lesion on the small penetrating arteries of the basal ganglia, thalamus and pons, whose rupture causes deep hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage?

explanations.A: Correct. Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are tiny aneurysmal dilatations of the small penetrating (lenticulostriate and other perforating) arteries, caused directly by chronic hypertension weakening the vessel media; their rupture is the classic mechanism of primary hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage, typically deep in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons or cerebellum. Their characteristic basal ganglia/thalamic distribution is why hypertensive bleeds are classically described as deep haemorrhages.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Berry (saccular) aneurysms occur at arterial branch points of the circle of Willis and classically cause subarachnoid haemorrhage, not deep hypertensive intraparenchymal bleeding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes lobar (peripheral cortical) haemorrhage in normotensive elderly patients, a distinct mechanism and distribution from hypertensive deep haemorrhage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arteriovenous malformations are congenital vascular anomalies that can bleed at any age, unrelated to chronic hypertensive vessel injury.

questions.learning_objective: State that Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms, caused by chronic hypertension, are the classic mechanism of deep hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.

questions.title: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) arises out of which sleep stage?
questions.question: Sleepwalking (somnambulism) is a disorder of arousal that classically arises out of which stage of sleep?

explanations.A: Correct. Sleepwalking is a disorder of arousal that arises out of slow-wave (stage N3) non-REM sleep, typically in the first third of the night when slow-wave sleep predominates, with motor tone preserved and impaired consciousness during the episode. Motor tone is preserved throughout the episode, unlike the atonia expected during REM sleep.
explanations.B: Incorrect. REM sleep is normally accompanied by near-total skeletal muscle atonia; complex ambulatory behaviour during REM instead characterises REM sleep behaviour disorder, a distinct condition from NREM sleepwalking.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stage N1 is the lightest stage of non-REM sleep and is not the classic stage from which sleepwalking arises.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stage N2 is an intermediate non-REM stage; sleepwalking is specifically linked to deep slow-wave (N3) sleep.

questions.learning_objective: State that sleepwalking is a disorder of non-REM (slow-wave) sleep, not REM sleep.

questions.title: Which artery passes deep to hyoglossus muscle?
questions.question: Which artery passes deep to (medial to) hyoglossus muscle on its way to supply the tongue?

explanations.A: Correct. The lingual artery, a branch of the external carotid artery, passes deep to hyoglossus muscle within the digastric triangle before continuing forward to supply the tongue — a key surgical landmark, since retracting hyoglossus is the standard step to expose and ligate the lingual artery. This deep relation is a key surgical landmark, since retracting hyoglossus is the standard step to expose and ligate the artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The facial artery passes superficial to (or grooves) the submandibular gland and crosses the mandible at the anterior border of masseter; it does not pass deep to hyoglossus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The maxillary artery passes through the infratemporal fossa, unrelated to the hyoglossus muscle in the neck.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The occipital artery courses deep to the posterior belly of digastric toward the scalp, not deep to hyoglossus.

questions.title: Which CNS tumour classically shows a clear perinuclear halo ("fried-egg" appearance) on formalin-fixed sections?
questions.question: Tumour cells showing a clear perinuclear halo ("fried-egg" appearance) on routine formalin-fixed histology are characteristic of which CNS neoplasm?

explanations.A: Correct. Oligodendroglioma cells show round, regular nuclei surrounded by a clear cytoplasmic halo on formalin-fixed sections, the classic "fried-egg" appearance — a fixation artefact from cytoplasmic swelling/clearing, characteristically absent on frozen section, and often accompanied by a "chicken-wire" capillary pattern. This halo is a fixation artefact from cytoplasmic swelling during processing, and is characteristically absent on frozen section.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glioblastoma shows necrosis and microvascular proliferation as its histologic hallmarks, not a perinuclear halo.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Medulloblastoma shows sheets of small, densely packed primitive (embryonal) cells, not the fried-egg halo pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Meningioma shows whorled cell arrangements and psammoma bodies, a distinct histological picture from the oligodendroglioma halo.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the clear perinuclear halo ("fried-egg" appearance) as the classic histological feature of oligodendroglioma on formalin-fixed sections.

questions.title: Haemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobe is classically caused by which CNS infection?
questions.question: Haemorrhagic necrosis localised to the medial temporal lobes is the classic imaging/pathology finding of which CNS infection?

explanations.A: Correct. Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis has a strong predilection for the medial temporal lobes, insula and orbitofrontal cortex, producing characteristic asymmetric haemorrhagic necrosis of these regions, explaining the classic presentation of temporal-lobe features such as olfactory hallucinations, personality change and seizures; empirical IV aciclovir is started immediately on suspicion because of its otherwise very high mortality. This localisation explains the classic presentation of fever, altered consciousness and temporal-lobe features such as olfactory hallucinations.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacterial meningitis produces diffuse leptomeningeal inflammation and purulent exudate, not focal temporal-lobe haemorrhagic necrosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy causes multifocal white-matter demyelination, not haemorrhagic necrosis localised to the temporal lobes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rabies encephalitis affects the brainstem and limbic system diffusely (Negri bodies in neurons) without the characteristic temporal-lobe haemorrhagic necrosis pattern of HSV encephalitis.

questions.learning_objective: State that herpes simplex encephalitis classically produces haemorrhagic necrosis localised to the temporal lobes.

questions.title: Which virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in immunocompromised patients?
questions.question: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, an oligodendrocyte-destroying demyelinating disease of immunocompromised patients, is caused by reactivation of which virus?

explanations.A: Correct. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by reactivation of JC virus, a human polyomavirus, in severely immunocompromised patients (e.g. advanced HIV/AIDS, or on drugs such as natalizumab); the virus lytically infects oligodendrocytes, producing multifocal demyelination with progressive focal deficits and no fever.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cytomegalovirus causes a different opportunistic CNS picture (e.g. CMV encephalitis/ventriculitis), not the oligodendrocyte-specific demyelination of PML.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Varicella-zoster virus can cause vasculopathy or encephalitis in immunocompromised patients but is not the cause of PML.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Measles virus (in its persistent form) causes subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a different demyelinating condition, not PML.

questions.learning_objective: Identify JC virus, a polyomavirus, as the cause of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in immunocompromised patients.

questions.title: Which structure forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle?
questions.question: Above the hypothalamic sulcus, which structure forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle?

explanations.A: Correct. The medial surface of the thalamus forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle above the hypothalamic sulcus, with the two thalami often joined across the ventricle by the interthalamic adhesion; this is why thalamic pathology can obstruct the third ventricle and cause hydrocephalus. The roof of the third ventricle, by contrast, is formed separately by the tela choroidea and its choroid plexus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hypothalamus forms the lower part of the lateral wall, below the hypothalamic sulcus, not the greater (upper) part attributed to the thalamus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The caudate nucleus lies lateral to the lateral ventricle, not forming the third ventricle's wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The internal capsule is a deep white-matter structure lateral to the thalamus and basal ganglia; it does not form the third ventricle's wall.

questions.learning_objective: State that the thalamus forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle (above the hypothalamic sulcus).

questions.title: The choroid plexus is composed of which two layers?
questions.question: The choroid plexus develops from, and is histologically composed of, which two layers?

options.A: Vascular pia mater (tela choroidea) covered by ependymal epithelium
options.B: Arachnoid mater covered by dura mater
options.C: Vascular pia mater covered by dura mater
options.D: Ependymal epithelium covered by arachnoid mater

explanations.A: Correct. The choroid plexus develops where vascular pia mater (the tela choroidea) invaginates into the ventricle and becomes covered by a single layer of specialised ependymal (choroidal epithelial) cells; each villus therefore has a pia-derived vascular core wrapped in ependymal-derived epithelium, which together allow active CSF secretion. This dual composition is what allows the choroidal epithelium to actively secrete cerebrospinal fluid from the plexus capillaries' filtrate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The arachnoid and dura mater are not the tissue layers forming the choroid plexus; the plexus is specifically pia-plus-ependyma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dura mater is not part of the choroid plexus; the epithelial covering is ependymal, not dural.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arachnoid mater is not part of the choroid plexus; the vascular core is pial, not arachnoid.

questions.learning_objective: State that the choroid plexus is composed of vascularised pia mater (tela choroidea) covered by ependymal epithelium.

questions.title: The medial geniculate body receives its main auditory input from which structure?
questions.question: In the auditory pathway, the medial geniculate body of the thalamus receives its principal ascending input via the brachium of which structure?

options.D: The nucleus of the lateral lemniscus

explanations.A: Correct. Ascending auditory fibres from the inferior colliculus of the midbrain leave via the brachium of the inferior colliculus and terminate in the medial geniculate body, the thalamic auditory relay nucleus, which then relays via the auditory radiation (through the sublentiform internal capsule) to the primary auditory cortex. From the medial geniculate body, third-order fibres form the auditory radiation en route to the primary auditory cortex.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior colliculus is a visual/oculomotor midbrain relay, not the source of the medial geniculate body's main auditory input.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral geniculate body is the visual thalamic relay, fed by the optic tract, functionally parallel to but distinct from the auditory medial geniculate body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nucleus of the lateral lemniscus is an earlier brainstem relay in the ascending auditory pathway, upstream of the inferior colliculus, not the direct input to the medial geniculate body.

questions.learning_objective: State that the medial geniculate body receives its principal input from the inferior colliculus via its brachium.

questions.title: The auditory radiation passes through which part of the internal capsule?
questions.question: The auditory radiation, carrying fibres from the medial geniculate body to the primary auditory cortex, passes through which part of the internal capsule?

explanations.A: Correct. The auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule, below the lentiform nucleus, on its way to the primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) — distinct from the mostly retrolentiform course of the optic radiation. This is classically contrasted with the mostly retrolentiform course of the optic radiation in the same internal capsule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The retrolentiform part, behind the lentiform nucleus, carries most of the optic radiation, not the auditory radiation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The genu of the internal capsule carries corticobulbar (corticonuclear) fibres for the face, not the auditory radiation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior limb carries frontopontine and thalamocortical fibres, not the auditory radiation.

questions.learning_objective: State that the auditory radiation passes through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule.

questions.title: Which cell type is found in the cerebellar cortex, not the cerebral cortex?
questions.question: Which large, GABAergic neuron type, forming the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, is found in the cerebellar cortex and NOT in the cerebral cortex?

explanations.A: Correct. Purkinje cells are large, flask-shaped GABAergic neurons confined to the molecular/Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellar cortex, forming its sole output to the deep cerebellar nuclei; they are not present in the cerebral cortex. They are not present in the cerebral cortex, whose principal projection neurons are instead pyramidal cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pyramidal cells are the principal projection neurons of the cerebral cortex, present in multiple cortical layers, unlike Purkinje cells which are cerebellum-specific.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stellate cells occur in both cerebral and cerebellar cortex as interneurons, so they are not the answer to a "cerebellum-only" cell-type question.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Granule cells occur in both the cerebellar cortex (granular layer) and parts of the cerebral cortex (e.g. dentate gyrus, some sensory areas), so they are not exclusive to the cerebellum.

questions.learning_objective: State that Purkinje cells are a cerebellar cortex cell type, not a cerebral cortex cell type.

questions.title: Which aphasia is characterised by an inability to repeat words despite fluent speech and preserved comprehension?
questions.question: A lesion of the arcuate fasciculus, disconnecting Wernicke's from Broca's area, produces which aphasia — fluent speech and intact comprehension, but a striking inability to repeat spoken words?

explanations.A: Correct. Conduction aphasia results from an arcuate fasciculus lesion disconnecting Wernicke's from Broca's area; patients have fluent speech and largely preserved comprehension but a striking, disproportionate inability to repeat spoken words, because comprehended content cannot be relayed for direct repetition. This selective repetition deficit, out of proportion to otherwise near-normal language function, is the hallmark distinguishing it from Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Broca's aphasia is non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension, from a lesion of Broca's area itself, not primarily a repetition-specific deficit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Wernicke's aphasia is fluent but meaningless (paraphasic) speech with poor comprehension, from a lesion of Wernicke's area — a broader deficit than the isolated repetition failure of conduction aphasia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Global aphasia involves severe impairment of both comprehension and production from a large dominant-hemisphere lesion, not the selective fluency-plus-comprehension-intact-but-repetition-impaired pattern of conduction aphasia.

questions.learning_objective: Identify impaired repetition, with preserved fluency and comprehension, as the hallmark of conduction aphasia.

questions.title: The excitatory reticular formation maintains cortical arousal chiefly through which property?
questions.question: The excitatory (ascending activating) component of the reticular formation maintains a baseline level of cortical arousal chiefly through which property?

options.A: Intrinsic, spontaneous (pacemaker-like) neuronal activity independent of sensory input
options.B: Activity entirely dependent on continuous incoming sensory input
options.C: Direct action potential conduction from the spinal cord dorsal columns
options.D: Rhythmic activity driven exclusively by the suprachiasmatic nucleus

explanations.A: Correct. The excitatory reticular formation, the core of the ascending reticular activating system, shows intrinsic, spontaneous pacemaker-like firing that does not require continuous sensory input, allowing it to maintain baseline cortical arousal even with reduced external stimulation — and explaining why anaesthetic/sedative agents can modulate arousal by acting directly on these neurons. This intrinsic excitability allows the reticular formation to maintain a baseline level of cortical arousal even with reduced external stimulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. If arousal depended entirely on ongoing sensory input, arousal would fail whenever sensory input was reduced, which is not the case; the reticular formation's intrinsic activity sustains a baseline level independent of input.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The reticular formation's arousal-maintaining activity is not simply relayed action potentials from the dorsal columns; it reflects the reticular neurons' own intrinsic excitability.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The suprachiasmatic nucleus governs circadian rhythm timing, not the reticular formation's moment-to-moment intrinsic excitatory activity.

questions.learning_objective: State that the excitatory reticular formation has intrinsic, spontaneous activity independent of sensory input.

questions.title: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle?
questions.question: Which thin sheet of grey matter, extending from the anterior commissure to the optic chiasm, forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle?

explanations.A: Correct. The lamina terminalis is a thin sheet of grey matter extending from the anterior commissure above to the optic chiasm below, forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle and closing off the rostral end of the neural tube at this level. It is functionally important as a boundary structure adjacent to the vascular organ of the lamina terminalis, a circumventricular organ.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tela choroidea forms the roof, not the anterior wall, of the third ventricle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The septum pellucidum separates the two lateral ventricles, not the third ventricle's anterior wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The interthalamic adhesion (massa intermedia) joins the two thalami across the third ventricle's lateral walls, not its anterior wall.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle.

questions.title: Which antibiotic class is given intrathecally for CNS infection because it penetrates the blood-brain barrier poorly by the IV route?
questions.question: Which antibiotic class, given for resistant Gram-negative CNS infection, is administered intrathecally because it penetrates the blood-brain barrier poorly when given intravenously?

explanations.A: Correct. Aminoglycosides are highly polar and cross the blood-brain barrier poorly even when meninges are inflamed, so for resistant Gram-negative CNS infection they are given intrathecally or intraventricularly, bypassing the barrier and achieving high local CSF concentrations while limiting systemic nephro-/ototoxicity. This bypasses the barrier entirely, achieving high local CSF concentrations while limiting systemic nephro- and ototoxicity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Third-generation cephalosporins achieve adequate CSF concentrations via the IV route alone when meninges are inflamed, and do not require the intrathecal route.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Penicillins, particularly at high IV doses, achieve therapeutic CSF levels in meningitis without requiring intrathecal administration.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Macrolides are not the antibiotic class classically singled out for poor blood-brain barrier penetration requiring intrathecal dosing in CNS infection.

questions.learning_objective: State that aminoglycosides are given intrathecally for CNS infection because of poor blood-brain barrier penetration by the IV route.

questions.title: The EEG chiefly reflects which type of electrical activity?
questions.question: The scalp-recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) chiefly reflects which type of underlying neuronal electrical activity?

options.A: Summated, spontaneous postsynaptic potentials of cortical pyramidal neurons
options.B: Individual axonal action potentials of cortical neurons
options.C: Muscle fibre action potentials from the scalp musculature
options.D: Direct current flow from the choroid plexus

explanations.A: Correct. The EEG reflects the summation of spontaneous excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials generated synchronously in the aligned apical dendrites of large populations of cortical pyramidal neurons; this synchronised graded synaptic activity, not individual spikes, produces the detectable scalp waveform. Individual axonal action potentials are too brief and poorly aligned to summate into a detectable scalp signal on their own.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Individual axonal action potentials are too brief and too asynchronous/poorly aligned to summate into a detectable scalp EEG signal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Scalp muscle activity is a recognised EEG artefact to be filtered out, not the intended physiological signal the EEG measures.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The choroid plexus produces CSF, not the electrical signal recorded by scalp EEG electrodes.

questions.title: Which induction anaesthetic is preferred in hypotensive or haemodynamically unstable patients?

explanations.A: Correct. This sympathomimetic profile makes it the preferred induction agent in hypotensive, hypovolaemic or haemodynamically unstable patients.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Propofol causes dose-dependent myocardial depression and vasodilation, worsening hypotension, so it is generally avoided as first choice in haemodynamically unstable patients.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thiopental similarly causes myocardial depression and vasodilation, making it a poor choice in hypotensive patients.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Halothane is a volatile inhalational agent that causes dose-dependent myocardial depression and hypotension, unlike ketamine's sympathomimetic profile.

questions.title: A lower motor neuron (bulbar) lesion produces which type of dysarthria?
questions.question: A lower motor neuron lesion of the bulbar musculature (e.g. bulbar palsy) produces which type of dysarthria, characterised by weak, hypernasal speech?

explanations.A: Correct. explanations.C: Incorrect. Ataxic dysarthria results from cerebellar dysfunction, producing irregular, scanning speech, not the weak, hypernasal pattern of an LMN lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypokinetic dysarthria results from basal ganglia dysfunction (e.g. Parkinson disease), producing soft, monotone speech, not the LMN, hypernasal pattern described.

questions.question: Electrical self-stimulation studies show that stimulation of which hypothalamic region produces aversive, fear-like ("punishment-centre") behavioural responses, in contrast to the lateral hypothalamic reward system?

questions.title: Which memory system stores general facts and "basic knowledge" about the world?
questions.question: Which declarative long-term memory system stores general facts and "basic knowledge" about the world, without reference to when or where it was learned?

explanations.A: Correct. Semantic memory is the declarative long-term memory store for general facts and "basic knowledge" (e.g. that Cairo is the capital of Egypt), held without reference to a specific personal learning event, and is relatively resistant to normal ageing and to some amnesias that preferentially disrupt episodic recall.

explanations.C: Incorrect. Procedural memory stores learned motor skills and habits (e.g. riding a bicycle), a non-declarative memory system, not general factual knowledge.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Working memory is a short-term, limited-capacity system for actively holding and manipulating information, not the long-term store of general knowledge.

questions.title: What is the term for the loss of memories formed before a brain injury?
questions.question: The loss of memories that were formed before a brain injury (e.g. head trauma), with a temporal gradient sparing more remote memories, is called what?

explanations.A: Correct. Retrograde amnesia is the inability to recall memories formed before the injury, reflecting disruption of previously consolidated (or still-consolidating) memory traces, and classically shows a temporal gradient in which more remote memories are better preserved than memories from just before the injury. Many amnestic syndromes after significant head trauma in fact produce a mixed picture with both retrograde and anterograde components.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after the injury, reflecting failure of ongoing consolidation rather than loss of pre-injury memories.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transient global amnesia is a distinct, self-limited clinical syndrome of sudden, temporary anterograde (and some retrograde) amnesia, not the general term for pre-injury memory loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dissociative amnesia is a psychiatric condition related to psychological trauma, not the physical-injury-related loss of pre-injury memories described.

questions.title: Which antidepressant is also approved for smoking cessation?
questions.question: Which norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI) antidepressant is also approved, under a separate brand, for smoking cessation?

explanations.A: Correct. questions.title: The sensory (dorsal horn) part of the developing spinal cord arises from which part of the neural tube?
questions.question: Embryologically, the sensory (dorsal horn, afferent) part of the developing spinal cord arises from which part of the neural tube?

explanations.A: Correct. The alar lamina, the dorsal division of the neural tube (separated from the ventral basal lamina by the sulcus limitans), gives rise to the sensory (afferent) dorsal horn neurons of the mature spinal cord, establishing the adult dorsal-sensory organisation. This dorsal-sensory, ventral-motor organisation established here is the developmental basis for the adult spinal cord's horn arrangement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The basal lamina, the ventral division, gives rise to the motor (efferent) ventral horn neurons, not the sensory dorsal horn.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The floor plate is a midline signalling structure at the ventral neural tube, not the source of sensory dorsal horn neurons.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While neural crest contributes to dorsal root ganglion (peripheral sensory neuron) cell bodies, the intrinsic dorsal horn neurons of the spinal cord itself arise from the alar lamina of the neural tube.

questions.title: CSF is absorbed into venous blood through which structure?
questions.question: Cerebrospinal fluid is reabsorbed into the venous blood of the dural sinuses (chiefly the superior sagittal sinus) through which structure?

explanations.A: Correct. CSF is reabsorbed into the venous circulation through arachnoid villi (and their larger clusters, arachnoid granulations), finger-like projections of the arachnoid mater into the venous sinuses (chiefly superior sagittal), which act as one-way pressure-sensitive valves; their obstruction is a classic cause of communicating hydrocephalus. These villi act as one-way pressure-sensitive valves, allowing CSF into venous blood while preventing back-flow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The choroid plexus is the site of CSF production, not absorption — the opposite end of CSF circulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ependymal lining lines the ventricles and central canal but is not the specific site of CSF venous absorption.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dural border cells are a layer within the dura mater, not the structure through which CSF drains into venous blood.

questions.title: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) produces spastic paralysis by blocking release of which neurotransmitters?
questions.question: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) cleaves synaptobrevin in spinal inhibitory interneurons, blocking release of which neurotransmitters and thereby producing spastic (not flaccid) paralysis?

explanations.A: Correct. Tetanospasmin travels retrogradely into inhibitory interneurons (including Renshaw cells) and cleaves synaptobrevin, blocking release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA; loss of this inhibitory restraint on motor neurons causes uncontrolled, simultaneous agonist/antagonist contraction — the sustained spasms of tetanus. This mechanism mirrors botulinum toxin's cleavage of similar vesicle-fusion proteins, though botulinum instead blocks excitatory transmission at the neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid rather than spastic paralysis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction is botulinum toxin's mechanism, producing flaccid (not spastic) paralysis, the opposite clinical picture from tetanus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory neurotransmitters; tetanus toxin's mechanism specifically blocks inhibitory transmitter release, not excitatory transmitters.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dopamine and serotonin are not the neurotransmitters whose blockade explains tetanus's spinal inhibitory-synapse mechanism.

questions.title: What does post-exposure rabies prophylaxis require in a previously unvaccinated person?

questions.title: A patient with renal cell carcinoma and a positive family history should raise suspicion for which syndrome?

questions.title: Which antipsychotic carries a risk of life-threatening agranulocytosis?
questions.question: Which atypical antipsychotic, reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, carries a risk of life-threatening agranulocytosis requiring regular blood count monitoring?

explanations.A: Correct. Clozapine, reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia because of its superior efficacy, carries a well-known risk of agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia), mandating regular absolute neutrophil count monitoring with dose interruption/discontinuation if counts fall below defined thresholds; this risk is why it is not first-line despite strong efficacy. The exact mechanism is thought to involve toxic or immune-mediated injury to bone marrow granulocyte precursors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Risperidone does not carry the defining agranulocytosis risk that mandates the specific monitoring protocol required for clozapine.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Olanzapine, another atypical antipsychotic, is not the agent classically singled out for agranulocytosis risk and mandatory blood count monitoring.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Haloperidol, a typical antipsychotic, is more associated with extrapyramidal side effects than with the defining agranulocytosis risk of clozapine.

questions.title: Which cranial nerve supplies motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue?
questions.question: Which cranial nerve supplies motor innervation to nearly all the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, with palatoglossus as the single exception?

explanations.A: Correct. The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies motor innervation to nearly all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus and intrinsic muscles); the single exception is palatoglossus, supplied instead by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus. A unilateral hypoglossal lesion causes ipsilateral tongue weakness with deviation toward the lesioned side on protrusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and motor to stylopharyngeus, not the tongue's own musculature.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The vagus nerve supplies only palatoglossus among the tongue muscles (via the pharyngeal plexus), not the majority of tongue musculature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The facial nerve supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (via chorda tympani) and facial expression muscles, not the tongue's intrinsic/extrinsic musculature.

questions.title: Which nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular ganglion?
questions.question: Which branch of the facial nerve joins the lingual nerve and carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular ganglion, supplying the submandibular and sublingual glands?

explanations.A: Correct. The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve carrying preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the superior salivatory nucleus, joins the lingual nerve and travels with it to the submandibular ganglion, where it synapses; postganglionic fibres then supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. It also carries taste fibres from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the pterygopalatine ganglion, supplying the lacrimal and nasal glands, not the submandibular ganglion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres (from the glossopharyngeal, inferior salivatory nucleus) to the otic ganglion, supplying the parotid gland, not the submandibular ganglion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland; it is not the nerve reaching the submandibular ganglion.

questions.title: Which glial cell type functions as the resident macrophage of the CNS?
questions.question: Which neuroectoderm-independent (mesodermal, monocyte-lineage) glial cell type functions as the resident phagocytic macrophage of the CNS?

explanations.A: Correct. Microglia derive from mesodermal yolk-sac myeloid progenitors, giving them a monocyte/macrophage lineage distinct from the other, neuroectoderm-derived glia; in their resting (ramified) state they survey the CNS, and on injury or infection they become phagocytic, clearing debris and pathogens and mounting an immune response. In their resting (ramified) state they continually survey the CNS parenchyma before becoming activated by injury or infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Astrocytes are neuroectoderm-derived cells providing structural support, blood-brain barrier maintenance and metabolic support to neurons, not macrophage-lineage phagocytes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Oligodendrocytes are neuroectoderm-derived cells that myelinate CNS axons, not the CNS's resident macrophages.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ependymal cells are neuroectoderm-derived cells lining the ventricles, involved in CSF-brain exchange, not phagocytic immune surveillance.

questions.title: The anterior nucleus of the thalamus receives input from which structure, via the mammillothalamic tract?
questions.question: As part of the Papez circuit, the anterior nucleus of the thalamus receives a major direct input via the mammillothalamic tract from which structure?

explanations.A: Correct. The anterior nucleus of the thalamus receives a major direct input from the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus via the mammillothalamic tract (tract of Vicq d'Azyr), one link of the Papez circuit; the anterior nucleus then projects onward to the cingulate gyrus. Lesions here (e.g. in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which damages the mammillary bodies) disrupt this relay and contribute to anterograde amnesia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hippocampus connects to the mammillary bodies via the fornix, not directly to the anterior thalamic nucleus; the mammillothalamic tract is a separate, later link in the circuit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The amygdala connects to the hypothalamus and septal area chiefly via the stria terminalis, not via the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The septal nuclei are connected to the hippocampus and hypothalamus via the fornix and other pathways, not via the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus.
